lead: A multimedia system is a stack, not one device. An authoring app edits media. Codecs compress and decompress. OS drivers control hardware. Hardware captures, stores and presents media. The stack exists because raw video and audio are too large and too fast for software alone. It is used in a phone camera, a video upload, an IRCTC announcement and a hospital scanner. Each layer hides the layer below: the editor asks a codec, the codec asks a driver, and the driver talks to the device.

blocks.text: The figure gives the working model. At the top is the authoring application: a video editor, audio editor or presentation tool. It never touches a camera register. Below it sit codecs and multimedia APIs. A codec is a coder-decoder: it converts raw pixels or samples to a compressed stream and back. An API is an application programming interface, a named set of calls such as “open camera” or “decode frame”. Below that are the operating system and drivers. A driver is software that knows a device’s control registers and data queues. At the bottom is hardware: CPU, GPU, camera, microphone, disk and display. The separation lets one editor work with many cameras. The cost is copying: data moves from camera buffer to system memory to GPU memory. A good system keeps that path short.

sections.h3: Capture, storage, display and the GPU

blocks.text: Capture devices turn a signal into numbers. A camera sensor gives a frame: a grid of pixels with colour samples. A microphone gives audio samples at a fixed sample rate. A scanner gives a still image line by line. Storage holds the result. A hard disk uses spinning platters; an SSD uses flash memory; an optical disk uses a laser. Hard disks are cheap per gigabyte, SSDs are fast, and optical disks suit archive but are slow. Displays present media: an LCD or OLED panel refreshes pixels, and a projector throws light on a screen. Audio devices include speakers, headphones and sound cards. A GPU is a graphics processing unit: many cores that draw pixels and run video encode and decode. A phone records H.264 or H.265 video in a dedicated block, so the CPU stays cool. USB carries data and also power to small devices; HDMI and audio cables carry signals between boxes. Only their role matters, not their protocols.

Software is layered too. A media player opens a container, finds streams and calls the right decoder. An editor adds cuts, titles and effects. An authoring tool arranges media into a presentation or game level. A codec library does compression. Multimedia APIs sit between applications and the OS: camera, audio and graphics APIs. Drivers sit below APIs. A typical capture-to-playback path has six steps.

items: App asks camera API for frames.
Driver copies sensor frames to memory.
Codec encodes video frames and audio samples.
Muxer writes streams into a container (see Chapter 4.5).
Player demuxes, decodes and presents with sync (see Chapter 4.9).

blocks.text: A slow driver drops frames; a missing codec refuses to play; a weak GPU stutters during effects. The fix is to find the layer that is late. The app never needs to know the file system.

figure.caption: The four layers each talk only to their neighbours: the editor asks the codec, the codec asks the driver, the driver drives the device. The codec layer is where the 2 h raw load of 1,345.0752 GB, 1080p30 video plus stereo audio, gets compressed.

examples.question: 1080p30 video uses 24 bits/pixel; stereo audio uses 48 kHz, 16 bits/sample; record for 2 h. Find raw GB (1 GB = 10^9 B) and one storage choice.
steps: Audio rate = 48,000 samples/s × 2 channels (stereo) × 2 B/sample (16 bits) = 192,000 B/s.
Total = 1,345.0752 GB; choose a 2 TB SSD.
examples.answer: Raw storage is 1,345.0752 GB (about 1.345 TB); use a 2 TB SSD and GPU video encode.

v = 1920*1080*3*30
vb = v*7200
a = 48000*2*2
ab = a*7200
t = (vb+ab)/1e9
print(v)
print(vb/1e9)
print(a)
print(ab/1e9)
print(t)

traps: 1080p30 is pixel size and frame rate, not file size.
16-bit audio is 2 bytes per sample, not 16.
1 GB is 10^9 B; 1 GiB is 2^30 B.
A container is not a codec; MP4 may hold H.264 and AAC.
GPU encode aids the CPU; it does not replace driver or CPU.

quiz.q: List the four layers of the working model.
quiz.a: Authoring app; codecs and APIs; OS and drivers; hardware.

quiz.q: Why call a camera API instead of reading the camera's registers directly?
quiz.a: The camera API hides the device details and returns frames in a standard pixel format, so the app works with any camera.

quiz.q: A player stutters on 4K only. Which layer and why?
quiz.a: GPU or codec; higher pixel rate overloads decode.

quiz.q: Byte rate for 48 kHz stereo 16-bit audio?
Why does hardware encode keep a phone cool?
quiz.a: A low-power block does it, not CPU cores.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phone chips now have neural units for video effects and noise removal. Cloud editors keep codecs and GPUs in data centres; thin clients only play streams. Search hardware video encode, GPU compute, Media Foundation, AVFoundation and GStreamer.
